{"id": "93:1/q09", "question": "What does the daylight-and-night pairing suggest about revelation and the Prophet?", "turns_on": "How the sensory alternation relates to revelation's pause, guidance, divine care and the oath's answer.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q09/p1", "position": "Alternation of light and night images revelation's pause and renewal without abandonment.", "reasons": "Razi and Nisaburi compare waxing and waning by divine wisdom with sending and withholding revelation. Bint al-Shati prefers the sensory analogy. Elmalili sees revealed knowledge and rest before renewal. Ibn al-Qayyim likens light after darkness to revelation after its pause, but Bint al-Shati says his lordship rationale misses the stated occasion. Al-Biqāʿī describes revelation's pause as a trial for the Prophet, who brings good in religion, this world and the afterlife."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p2", "position": "Day is revelation and guidance; night suggests recitation, reflection and calm.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says nearby idolaters heard the Prophet's night recitation and cites 73:2-3. Qutb sees a tender setting where the spirit senses creation worshipping, cosmic companionship and graceful musical cadence. Kuranyolu reports Ibn Ashur's sunlight analogy. Ibn ʿĀshūr ties the night qualification to the Prophet's night prayer in 73:2–3, whose recitation nearby polytheists heard."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p3", "position": "The contrast answers the disbelievers' unsupported taunt.", "reasons": "Razi and Nisaburi say the taunters could not prove abandonment. Ibn Ashur says the oath targets their inference from missed night recitation, while the Prophet himself had no doubt. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the oath's emphasis indirectly rebukes the polytheists because the Prophet did not doubt God's report."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p4", "position": "Light and dark illustrate changing spiritual and epistemic states.", "reasons": "Biqa'i applies mixed and pure light to clear and ambiguous teachings, bright hearts and darkening appetite; obscurity can yield certainty through remembering signs and seeking refuge. Bint al-Shati relates the senses to guidance or falsehood; Razi/Nisaburi say all creatures undergo change."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p5", "position": "Night's rest and day's work together are divine mercy.", "reasons": "Islahi cites 10:67 and 28:73. Abduh says quiet night restores strength after first revelation; Bint al-Shati says that account nearly loses the sensory analogy."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p6", "position": "The contrast visibly demonstrates the Creator's power.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir relates this pairing to 92:1-2 and 6:96."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p7", "position": "Day and night model developmental trials leading to relief and duties.", "reasons": "Islahi traces movement from the models to reassurance, better times, past help and duties arising from favor."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p8", "position": "Earlier explanations fail to connect the oath clearly to its answer.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati faults Tabari, Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan for lacking a clear connection and for not comparing explicit Qur'anic denials of oaths."}, {"id": "93:1/q09/p9", "position": "The day-and-night oath testifies to God's favor and honor of the Prophet, affirming prophethood, resurrection, and recompense.", "reasons": "Itqan says the oath by forenoon and night bears witness to God's favor and honor of the Prophet and thereby confirms his prophethood and the resurrection and recompense."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q10", "question": "Why does this sūra place day before night?", "turns_on": "Whether the order emphasizes daylight's honor, the duration of joy and sorrow, or moral stages.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q10/p1", "position": "Brief joy is set against much longer sorrow.", "reasons": "Bursawi equates one forenoon hour to the whole night as Muhammad equals all prophets. He cites a cloud raining grief for 300 years versus a cloud raining joy for an hour. Bint al-Shati reports the Razi/Nisaburi prophet comparison."}, {"id": "93:1/q10/p2", "position": "Day leads here for its inherent and contextual honor.", "reasons": "Bursawi says night precedes in al-Layl because darkness is the original state; sunlight makes day, then air returns to darkness at sunset. He cites 6:1. Al-Biqāʿī calls forenoon the noblest, gentlest and most luminous period of the day."}, {"id": "93:1/q10/p3", "position": "Life is preferred before warning of despair and divine plotting.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati reports an interpretation giving this staged moral order."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q11", "question": "What interrupted revelation before this sūra?", "turns_on": "The reports name different circumstances before revelation resumed.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q11/p1", "position": "Illness prevented night prayer for one or two, or two or three, nights.", "reasons": "Jundub's versions vary. Ibn Ashur understands the taunt as a reaction to absent nighttime Quran recitation. Al-Itqān cites the report in both Ṣaḥīḥ collections; Ibn Ḥajar prefers it to the puppy account."}, {"id": "93:1/q11/p2", "position": "Gabriel or revelation paused, with no precipitating cause specified.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Khalawayh, Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, Durr, Suyuti, Qutb and Study Quran relate pause and ensuing taunt. Qutb says Gabriel's visits sustained the Prophet through rejection and persecution, so absence distressed him. Ibn al-Jazarī treats the pause reported by Jundub as firmly established; al-Tirmidhī grades the report cited by Ibn ʿĀshūr ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Al-Durr identifies reports from Qatāda and al-Ḍaḥḥāk as mursal."}, {"id": "93:1/q11/p3", "position": "A puppy or dead puppy was in the Prophet's house.", "reasons": "Zayd ibn Aslam says Gabriel explained angels avoid a house with a dog or image. Khawla and Umm Hafs locate a dead puppy under the bed and give four days. Ibn Hajar says a puppy-related delay is known, but rejects this as the cause of the sūra because it conflicts with sound reports. Al-Itqān's Khawla report says a dead puppy beneath a bed kept Gabriel away; Ibn Ḥajar calls the causal attribution strange because its chain has an unknown narrator."}, {"id": "93:1/q11/p4", "position": "The Prophet promised answers to Jewish questions without saying 'if God wills'.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi name Dhu al-Qarnayn, the Cave Companions and the Spirit."}, {"id": "93:1/q11/p5", "position": "A stone injured the Prophet's finger, after which he missed night prayer.", "reasons": "A second Jundub version gives two or three nights. Ibn Kathir calls the injury authentic but the causal link unusual; Durr cites Tirmidhi's authentication. Ibn Kathīr accepts the finger verse as authentic in the two Ṣaḥīḥ collections but calls its role as the sūra's cause unusual; Ibn al-Jazarī likewise questions that causal link. Al-Tirmidhī graded the finger report cited by al-Durr authentic."}, {"id": "93:1/q11/p6", "position": "The Prophet or companions neglected grooming.", "reasons": "Tha'labi reports the Prophet referring to unclean spaces between fingers and untrimmed nails; Ibn al-Jawzi lists a companion's lack of cleanliness."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q12", "question": "How long was the reported interruption?", "turns_on": "The transmitted numerical counts differ.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q12/p1", "position": "Forty days or mornings.", "reasons": "Muqatil gives forty days; Ibn Khalawayh cites forty mornings; Baghawi and Study Quran include forty."}, {"id": "93:1/q12/p2", "position": "Twelve days.", "reasons": "Ibn Jurayj gives twelve; Baghawi repeats it and Study Quran includes it."}, {"id": "93:1/q12/p3", "position": "Four days.", "reasons": "Umm Hafs and Khawla give four days in the dead-puppy account."}, {"id": "93:1/q12/p4", "position": "Fifteen days.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas gives fifteen; Baghawi repeats it."}, {"id": "93:1/q12/p5", "position": "Twenty-five days.", "reasons": "Tha'labi transmits this number without a named transmitter."}, {"id": "93:1/q12/p6", "position": "Fifty days.", "reasons": "Study Quran includes fifty among the reports."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q13", "question": "Who voiced the claim that the Prophet had been abandoned?", "turns_on": "Whether the speaker was hostile, compassionate, or identified as a cousin's daughter.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q13/p1", "position": "Polytheists or Quraysh collectively.", "reasons": "Their taunt follows Gabriel's delay; Razi/Nisaburi say they lacked proof, and Ibn Ashur ties their insinuation to missed nighttime recitation."}, {"id": "93:1/q13/p2", "position": "A woman, identified in some accounts as Umm Jamil, Abu Lahab's wife.", "reasons": "Jundub calls her a woman. Tha'labi, Baghawi, Ibn Ishaq via Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Zayd ibn Arqam name Umm Jamil. She calls his companion a devil or Satan. Durr places her confrontation after Sūrat Abī Lahab. Ibn Hajar says her remark was spiteful. Al-Durr's Zayd ibn Arqam account places Abū Lahab's wife's taunt after Sūrat al-Masad. Ibn ʿĀshūr doubts Jundub could have heard her taunt, given his age and possible post-Hijra conversion, and suspects two reports were joined."}, {"id": "93:1/q13/p3", "position": "Khadija spoke with concern over apparent rejection.", "reasons": "Abdullah ibn Shaddad and Urwa transmit her remark after a pause or distress. Ibn Hajar distinguishes compassion from Umm Jamil's spite. Tha'labi relates this to the first pause after al-Alaq. The later reports are mursal. Ibn Kathīr notes that the two Khadīja reports are mursal and that attribution to her may be unpreserved or express sorrow."}, {"id": "93:1/q13/p4", "position": "A cousin's daughter said his companion had left him.", "reasons": "Durr's Jundub report gives this identification."}]}

{"id": "93:1/q15", "question": "How should the following phrase about night be understood beside this oath?", "turns_on": "Whether sajā means arrival, departure or stillness.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q15/p1", "position": "Night settles, darkens, or grows still among its people.", "reasons": "Tabrisi cites poetry about a calm sea and night; Ibn Kathir adds darkness. Durr reports Qatada's quiet people. Bint al-Shati reports Tabari, Zamakhshari and Abduh on stillness. Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Aʿshā's calm sea, a rajaz line on a calm night, and Jarīr's still eyes as lexical evidence; al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Aṣmaʿī describe night covering the day like cloth, while al-Ḥasan and Ibn ʿAbbās speak of darkness covering everything. Ibn ʿĀshūr says night stretches and darkness lasts; he gives sajā a wāw root."}, {"id": "93:1/q15/p2", "position": "Night arrives.", "reasons": "Durr gives Ibn Abbas's gloss; Bint al-Shati includes this among Tabari's reported alternatives."}, {"id": "93:1/q15/p3", "position": "Night departs.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati lists this among Tabari's reported alternatives."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q16", "question": "Where and when in the revelation sequence was this sūra revealed?", "turns_on": "The notes preserve different revelation-order lists and first-complete-sūra claims.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q16/p1", "position": "It is Meccan.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Abu Hayyan, Durr, Ibn Abbas, Alusi and Bint al-Shati affirm Meccan origin; Study Quran calls it early Meccan. Bint al-Shati says there is no disagreement. Al-Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Qurṭubī, al-Ālūsī and Ibn ʿĀshūr state that the Meccan classification is agreed upon."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p2", "position": "It followed al-ʿAlaq after Gabriel's first pause.", "reasons": "Abdullah ibn Shaddad gives this order and Khadija's concern."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p3", "position": "It followed 'Read', al-Muddaththir and al-Qalam through 68:4.", "reasons": "Tha'labi gives this sequence."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p4", "position": "It is commonly eleventh, after al-Fajr.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shati gives this revelation rank. Ibn ʿĀshūr places it immediately before al-Inshirāḥ."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p5", "position": "It is fourth in one list or seventh in another.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports both rankings, which vary in the note."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p6", "position": "It may be the first sūra revealed whole.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this and the competing assignment to al-Fatiha."}, {"id": "93:1/q16/p7", "position": "It was revealed when Gabriel appeared in his created form and descended at al-Abṭaḥ.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr attributes this account to Ibn Isḥāq and other early authorities and links it to 53:10."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q17", "question": "How many verses does the sūra have?", "turns_on": "Different verse counts.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q17/p1", "position": "Eleven verses.", "reasons": "Durr gives eleven; Alusi calls eleven unanimous."}, {"id": "93:1/q17/p2", "position": "Ten verses.", "reasons": "Baghawi gives ten."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q18", "question": "How is takbīr recited from this sūra onward?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q18/p1", "position": "Say Allāhu akbar at each sūra ending from al-Ḍuḥā through the Qur'an's end.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir's practice includes the basmala; Durr reports a Prophetic instruction. Ibn Khalawayh links the practice with the Prophet's joy when Gabriel returned. Ibn Kathīr says al-Bazzī alone transmitted the raised report; Abū Ḥātim and al-ʿUqaylī weakened him, and Ibn Khuzayma suspected a missing transmitter. Ibn al-Jazarī answers that many reliable narrators took it from al-Bazzī, although routes differ between Prophetic and Companion attribution. Al-Shāfiʿī praised its use in prayer as Sunnah. Al-Ḥalīmī compares it to magnifying God at Ramadan's completion; others see it marking the felt end of revelation. Sulaym al-Rāzī requires pauses around the formula. Ibn al-Jazarī records wider Meccan transmission, and al-Dānī describes continuing after al-Nās with al-Fātiḥa and 2:1–5 before the completion prayer. Al-Dānī rejects an inserted Sufyān in one chain. Ibn Jurayj recommends it inside and outside congregational prayer, and reports describe its use in Ramadan."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p2", "position": "Begin takbīr at the end of Sūrat al-Layl.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr reports this start among some reciters."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p3", "position": "Begin takbīr at the opening of al-Ḍuḥā.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān describes this as the Meccan reading; al-Itqān reports the disputed starting point, whereas Ibn al-Jazarī says he found no authority for this start."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p4", "position": "Use the longer formula including lā ilāha illā Allāh before Allāhu akbar.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and al-Itqān report this alongside the shorter Allāhu akbar formula; al-Sakhāwī and Abū Shāma allow it inside and outside prayer."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p5", "position": "Do not use takbīr as a regular recitation formula.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports concern that listeners may mistake it for Qur'anic text; Ibn al-Jazarī reports other transmitters from al-Sūsī without takbīr and Abū al-Fatḥ saying omission is blameless."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p6", "position": "Make takbīr at the beginning of every sūra for all readers.", "reasons": "Al-Hudhalī reports al-Dīnawarī's practice; Ibn al-Jazarī also mentions authorities who adopted takbīr for all readers or every sūra opening."}, {"id": "93:1/q18/p7", "position": "Use takbīr at completion of the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Ahwāzī calls it a transmitted Meccan practice in recitation and prayer; Sufyān ibn ʿUyayna reports Ṣadaqa ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Kathīr doing so for more than seventy years."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q19", "question": "What reward is reported for reciting the sūra?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q19/p1", "position": "Intercession and reward for every orphan and asker.", "reasons": "Jishumi transmits a Prophetic report through Ubayy scaling the reward to every such person."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q20", "question": "How does this sūra connect to its neighbors?", "turns_on": "The relation to the preceding and following sūras is explained in different ways.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q20/p1", "position": "It follows al-Layl's most God-fearing figure with the Prophet and God's favors to him.", "reasons": "Jishumi links earlier reward to the Prophet's resurrection honor; Abu Hayyan and Alusi cite 92:17. Biqa'i makes enduring favor through perfected qualities the theme and daylight its sign. Al-Biqāʿī says the Prophet, as the most pious, receives the earlier sūra's promise in the form of consolation during revelation's pause."}, {"id": "93:1/q20/p2", "position": "Sūras 93 and 94 are a pair moving from opposition toward success.", "reasons": "Islahi distinguishes intense Meccan opposition from emerging success; Study Quran distinguishes external needs here from spiritual relief in 94, both recalling favor and duties. Abū Shāma counts the following Sūrat al-Inshirāḥ among six sūras with interrogative openings."}, {"id": "93:1/q20/p3", "position": "Al-Layl concerns Abu Bakr; this sūra concerns the Messenger, with no intervening sūra.", "reasons": "Alusi reports the Imam's inference of closeness, while denying precedence implies superiority; he rejects the Imam's flower metaphor. The Imam denies that al-Layl's precedence implies Abū Bakr's superior rank, appealing to oath order and other examples; al-Ālūsī finds the Imam's accompanying spring-flower analogy weak."}, {"id": "93:1/q20/p4", "position": "Sūras 93 and 94 may once have been a single sūra.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports Companions reciting them in one prayer cycle without an intervening basmala."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q21", "question": "What is the sūra's central assurance?", "turns_on": "Whether it is framed as specific consolation or a broad account of perfected piety.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q21/p1", "position": "God has not abandoned the Prophet and will keep favoring and consoling him.", "reasons": "Qutb describes hope, closeness and calm amid persecution, future reward, and past care as proof. Study Quran adds care for the vulnerable and proclamation of God's gifts. Ibn Ashur says past care proves continuing care; Islahi traces better times and duties; Jishumi includes honor at resurrection. Itqan says the day-and-night oath attests God's favor and honor of the Prophet, and thereby affirms his prophethood, resurrection, and recompense. Ibn ʿĀshūr connects the assurance to a better Hereafter, divine care through childhood and maturity, and gratitude expressed in service and praise. Al-Durr reports the Prophet's response that his Lord is gracious and worthy of bestowing favor."}, {"id": "93:1/q21/p2", "position": "The most God-fearing remains in divine favor through perfected qualities.", "reasons": "Biqa'i identifies this purpose and reads the daylight title as spiritual light of perfected character. Al-Biqāʿī identifies the Prophet as the most pious and mentions Abū Bakr as first among the pious after him."}]}

{"id": "95:4/q01", "question": "What statement answers the opening oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q01/p1", "position": "God's declaration that He created humanity in the best constitution answers the oath.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari and Qatadah identify the oath's answer; al-Tabari cites the fig and olive. {"id": "95:4/q02", "question": "Why is God explicitly named as the creator?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q02/p1", "position": "The active divine subject displays God's power, artistry, blessing, and authority to guide the humans He made.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai compares active wording in 7:181 and 36:71–72 with passive creation statements about weakness in 4:28, 21:37, and 70:19–21; the Creator knows the fitting way of life."}]}
{"id": "95:4/q03", "question": "What does God's creating humanity describe here?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is origination of the species, each person's formation, or the act of divine determination.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q03/p1", "position": "God brought the human species into being through its first origin and the causes of reproduction.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur cites 38:75 and 7:11 for first creation and subsequent shaping; al-Biqa'i stresses divine might."}, {"id": "95:4/q03/p2", "position": "The verse most likely describes each person's formation in the womb.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum cites human developmental language in 86:5–6, 80:18–19, 75:38, 77:20, and 70:39."}]}
{"id": "95:4/q04", "question": "Whom does 'the human' denote?", "turns_on": "Whether the definite singular is generic, names the original human essence, or points to a particular person.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q04/p1", "position": "Humanity as a species, including men and women, believers and unbelievers, or Adam and his descendants.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi says the singular can be collective; al-Alusi cites the connected exception in 95:6. Ibn Ashur also allows the original human essence apart from individual changes, comparing 70:19, a proverb, and poetry. Spelling varies."}, {"id": "95:4/q04/p3", "position": "Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi attributes this to Ata; al-Qurtubi connects it with an unbelieving human."}, {"id": "95:4/q04/p4", "position": "An unbeliever, as the subsequent lowering concerns deniers of resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi explicitly relates the reading to resurrection denial. {"id": "95:4/q05", "question": "What does taqwīm mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q05/p1", "position": "Shaping, straightening, ordering, or adjusting something into its fitting, balanced condition.", "reasons": "Al-Razi and Ibn Ashur define it as giving a thing the form it ought to have. Ibn Atiyya says the adjective must modify a stated or understood noun; al-Samin sees no need for more complex analyses. Al-Samin regards the complication as unnecessary."}, {"id": "95:4/q06/p3", "position": "Fī is extra, leaving an absolute object: God shaped him with the best shaping.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa and a reported parsing in al-Alusi allow it; al-Samin says it is unnecessary."}, {"id": "95:4/q06/p4", "position": "Fī figuratively conveys secure attachment or possession of the excellent constitution.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says it works like bāʾ of accompaniment or lām of possession, lending force concisely."}, {"id": "95:4/q06/p5", "position": "The phrase is a circumstantial description; taqwīm denotes the resulting constitution, rather than God's act of forming.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa distinguishes the creature's state from the Creator's action."}]}

{"id": "95:4/q08", "question": "How broadly does 'best' rank humanity?", "turns_on": "Whether it asserts absolute superiority to all created forms or fitness relative to humanity's purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q08/p1", "position": "Humanity is the most excellent and beautiful of creatures.", "reasons": "Some scholars universalize the comparison; al-Qurtubi says no created thing is more beautiful and al-Islahi and Kur'an Yolu stress humanity's high rank. {"id": "95:4/q09", "question": "What does the verse imply about God's form and Adam being made in His image?", "turns_on": "How to understand shared attributes without making God bodily.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q09/p1", "position": "God has no bodily form; the Adam-image report refers to attributes or meanings such as life, knowledge, power, will, speech, hearing, and sight.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri reasons that if form were shared with creation, its perfection would belong to God; yet the verse calls human form best. {"id": "95:4/q11", "question": "What does the verse teach about human potential and decline?", "turns_on": "How initial excellence relates to later choice, corruption, and divine reward.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q11/p1", "position": "Humans are made capable of truth and ascent, yet desire, pride, and rejecting guidance can bring them low; believers retain the reward of faith and good action.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i says reason can lead from Hell to Paradise while appetite and anger explain corruption (2:30); human form alone cannot save. {"id": "95:4/q12", "question": "What reports about the comparison with the moon and a conditional divorce are given?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse proves the wife is more beautiful than the moon, and how the oath's condition is framed.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q12/p1", "position": "The conditional divorce did not take effect, since the verse calls the human the best or most beautiful creation.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya reports some jurists; al-Razi, al-Qurtubi, Bursevi, Elmalili, and al-Alusi name Yahya ibn Aktham and some Hanafis. {"id": "95:4/q13", "question": "How is the verse linked to the rest of the surah and neighboring surahs?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q13/p1", "position": "The oath, the human capacity for truth, the fall, and the believers' exception form a moral sequence.", "reasons": "Al-Samarrai says revelation's places point to guidance suited to human nature and that creation and decline support resurrection and judgment. Ibn Ashur says the sacred places suggest stages of divine law and shared foundations; the surah warns rejecters and recalls God's gift. Kur'an Yolu sees fig and olive as food, Sinai as revelation, Mecca as security. Study Quran says sites of revelation support reading human stature as receptivity to revelation. Al-Gharnati praises formation from semen and readiness for revelation. Al-Wahidi notes that the secure city's protection extends to residents and visitors. Al-Samarrai reads thumma as delay and rank contrast and compares al-Inshiqaq's toil with al-Tin's honoring of humanity."}, {"id": "95:4/q13/p2", "position": "The surah follows al-Sharh's account of Muhammad by considering the human kind and its possible rise or fall.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i names Muhammad as the finest human, Abraham the noblest root, and Mecca the best land; Abu Hayyan describes opponents being lowered while mankind is prepared for truth. Al-Alusi says the previous surah showed the Prophet's perfected creation and character."}, {"id": "95:4/q13/p3", "position": "The surah's account of creation and religion summarizes its predecessors and prepares for the next surah's command to read.", "reasons": "Elmalili relates the transition to true religion and God as best judge."}, {"id": "95:4/q13/p4", "position": "The oath evokes Sinai, Seir, and Paran and a summary of Torah history.", "reasons": "Al-Biqa'i links ideal creation, the righteous, and the fallen with the Torah's beginning, laws, and later history."}, {"id": "95:4/q13/p5", "position": "The believers' reward amid old age connects this surah with the account in 103:3.", "reasons": "Al-Baghawi relates Ibrahim's explanation that elderly believers retain credit for good works to 95:4–6."}]}
{"id": "95:4/q14", "question": "What ancillary reports about this surah's setting and recitation occur?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q14/p1", "position": "Most call the surah Meccan, while reports from Ibn Abbas and Qatadah call it Medinan.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi argues that the secure city as Mecca supports the majority, says the name is also al-Tin, and reports agreement on eight verses; Study Quran calls it early-middle Meccan after surah 85; Asad also places it after surah 85."}, {"id": "95:4/q14/p2", "position": "The Prophet recited Surat al-Tin in one of the two evening prayer rak'ahs while traveling.", "reasons": "Ibn Hibban transmits the report from al-Bara ibn Azib."}]}

{"id": "95:4/q16", "question": "What ancillary claims about Qur'anic eloquence are recorded?", "turns_on": "Whether excellence lies in meaning-led expression, composition, rare diction, sound pattern, or broader content.", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q16/p1", "position": "Qur'anic eloquence is meaningful expression in the best verbal form, with harmonious wording and arrangement.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani ranks its eloquence at the highest miraculous level and lists ten branches; al-Khattabi describes word, meaning, and their organizing bond and says the Qur'an perfects all three across creed, law, ethics, and reports. Bint al-Shati records their differing accounts of levels, and al-Baqillani's combination of meanings and wording. Al-Jurjani says trained judgment detects subtle compositional merit, illustrated by al-Buhturi's reports and Ibn al-Mu'tazz's verse."}, {"id": "95:4/q16/p2", "position": "Qur'anic endings are eloquent when meaning leads the sound; forced saj' reverses that order.", "reasons": "Al-Rummani contrasts fawasil with saj', giving the soothsayer and Musaylima as poor examples, and allows identical or nearby ending letters when context keeps meanings clear. Bint al-Shati prefers his account, questions al-Baqillani's clause-length distinction, and says allowing saj' does not entail sarfah."}, {"id": "95:4/q16/p3", "position": "Rare vocabulary, mere correctness, and pronunciation do not explain the Qur'an's inimitability.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says people familiar with rare words could answer in kind, while challenging others would be like asking Arabs to speak Turkish. Umar's praise of Zuhayr and anecdotes about al-Hajjaj, Yahya ibn Ya'mar, and poetic transmission illustrate the limits of obscurity and routine parsing. Metaphor works by asserting the borrowed quality itself, rather than merely substituting a label; he cites 12:31 and lion, king, and musk examples."}, {"id": "95:4/q16/p4", "position": "Some locate the miracle in the Qur'an's values, parables, and laws; Bint al-Shati questions whether this accounts for the early challenge.", "reasons": "She observes that the Meccan challenge preceded the completion of legislation and records al-Khattabi and al-Baqillani linking meanings with wording."}]}
{"id": "95:4/q17", "question": "What other linguistic and textual observations are included?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "95:4/q17/p1", "position": "The codices were checked, and reports of scribal error can refer to dialect or choice among allowed ahruf.", "reasons": "Al-Suyuti reconciles reports about Umar, Uthman, and Aisha by proposing an early correction of non-Quraysh spelling such as al-tabuwah for al-tabut. {"id": "95:5/q01", "question": "What does being returned to the lowest of the low mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the descent names an observable bodily reversal, a final place or form of punishment, or corruption of the human's original moral disposition; the following exception is a major test.", "positions": [{"id": "95:5/q01/p1", "position": "Return to decrepit old age, with bodily weakness and sometimes lost reason.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿIkrima, Ibrāhīm, Qatāda and others describe strength, beauty, senses, movement, voice and intellect ebbing; 16:70, 22:5 and 36:68 parallel the reversal. Al-Ṭabarī prefers this visible change because even deniers see aging, whereas they deny Hell; it proves resurrection (95:7). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī liken the elder to a child. Al-Farrāʾ and Ibn ʿAṭiyya say generic humanity need not imply every individual ages so far. Ibn Qutayba, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī and al-Baghawī compare the weak, ill and children, with senile elders lower still. Al-Zamakhsharī and al-Nasafī detail bent backs, white hair, wrinkled skin, weakened senses and gait; Abū Ḥayyān calls that elaboration excessive. Bursawī cites a Persian poem; Corpus Coranicum cites Qurʾanic usage, Arabic poetry and radda against Birkeland's Hell argument. Al-Ḥākim authenticated the Ibn ʿAbbās report on reciters according to al-Durr. Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that bodily aging ill fits the emphatic oath and the sūra's purpose; Ibn Kathīr and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī object that believers also age, making the apparent exception difficult. Baghawī connects Ibrāhīm's explanation of continuing reward in old age to the sequence from excellent creation through lowering and the believers' exception. Ibn ʿAbbās' report also says the human was first made upright rather than face-down before reaching old age. Ibn ʿĀshūr objects that the senility reading fits the sūra's purpose poorly and hardly warrants an oath."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p2", "position": "God casts the unbeliever into Hell or its lowest depths.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid, Abū al-ʿĀliya, Ibn Zayd and others transmit this reading. ʿAlī describes Hell's gates as descending and being filled from below. Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr and others cite the connected exception for believers and compare 103:2–3; al-Qushayrī says the general opening then narrows to disbelievers. Al-Nuḥḥās reports al-Ṭabarī's opposing argument: the audience witnesses aging but denies the Fire. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 4:145 for the lowest depth. Birkeland argues ordinary aging cannot explain exceptional humiliation, but Corpus Coranicum rejects his conclusion. Ibn ʿAbbās' reported poem of ʿAlī uses the phrase for the depth near Hell. Abū al-ʿĀliya specifies that the person in Hell has the worst image. Qatāda reads the oath's answer as 95:4 and the later judgment question as a call to certainty because God's proof has come."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p3", "position": "The person becomes one of Hell's people, hideous in form; some reports specify the form of a pig.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Nasafī, al-Bayḍāwī and al-Ālūsī connect the ugliness to ingratitude for fine creation. Abū al-ʿĀliya specifically reports a pig form, while other descriptions say the ugliest shape without naming an animal. Al-Ālūsī favors the Judgment Day reading as most contextual. Bursawī says inner traits become outward forms at resurrection; Ibn Burjān adds an animal or vermin form in the intermediate realm and disfigurement afterward. Abū al-ʿĀliya joins the worst bodily image specifically to being in Hell."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p4", "position": "People fall into disbelief, misguidance, and moral or spiritual baseness.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj and al-Qurṭubī compare humanity's loss and believers' exception in 103:2–3. Al-Biqāʿī says desire defeats reason, prompting idolatry, injustice and falsehood; rational people thus sink beneath unaccountable beasts and deserve punishment. Quṭb similarly contrasts animals' faithfulness to their nature with humans' capacity to rise even beyond angels, citing the Ascension. Ibn ʿĀshūr locates the baseness especially in belief: idolatry, deifying time and denying the Creator despite 51:21, and lists human sacrifice, infanticide and burning widows among its moral results. Al-Qāshānī depicts the veiled soul imprisoned in nature. Al-Iṣlāḥī invokes choice, innate guidance and consequent divine humiliation. Samarrai also includes the unbeliever's distressed earthly life, citing 20:124 and 22:31. Asad ascribes decline to human acts and omissions; al-Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr stress the initial sound disposition."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p5", "position": "For the disbeliever, decline runs from youth to age and finally to Hell.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās gives this successive course and adduces a line attributed to ʿAlī using the low expression for a depth by Hell."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p6", "position": "The lowest are idolaters, while the human in the preceding clause is Muḥammad.", "reasons": "Al-Durr explicitly marks this Ibn ʿAbbās report weak; it also calls the four caliphs the following exception and assigns geographical senses to the oaths."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p7", "position": "Human arrogance is brought low through bodily filth that recalls created dependence.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī's reported explanation compares pretensions to divinity with Pharaoh's claim in 79:24; humiliation restores awareness of God's decree."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p8", "position": "The basest person exploits another person's religion for gain.", "reasons": "In Mālik's report, Rabīʿa approved this answer; Ibn ʿĀshūr applies it to polytheist leaders who secured power by misleading their followers into idol worship."}, {"id": "95:5/q01/p9", "position": "The phrase can embrace age, Hell, moral decline, and distress together.", "reasons": "Samarrai says the wording admits all transmitted readings; the verse endings intentionally carry multiple senses. Elmalılı traces a broad reversal of purity, health, knowledge and dignity into weakness, ignorance, pain, death and Hell."}]}

{"id": "95:5/q03", "question": "How does رَدَدْنَٰهُ construe the descent?", "turns_on": "Whether radda denotes a change of state with two objects, a one-object verb plus circumstantial description, or motion to a place.", "positions": [{"id": "95:5/q03/p1", "position": "Radda means make or render, taking the pronoun and asfal as two objects.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī cites a poetic line for the construction. {"id": "95:5/q04", "question": "To whom does the pronoun in رَدَدْنَٰهُ refer?", "turns_on": "Whether al-insān in 95:4 is a generic human or a specific person, and whether a general opening narrows to unbelievers.", "positions": [{"id": "95:5/q04/p1", "position": "The human being mentioned in the previous verse, used generically for humankind.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly identifies the antecedent and says its two earlier senses carry through.
